topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain why atoms of the same element can have different mass numbers. (3)
hints: Mass number counts protons and neutrons.
questions.solution:
Atoms of the same element have the same number of protons. [B1]
They can have different numbers of neutrons. [B1]
Atoms with the same proton number but different neutron numbers are isotopes, so their mass numbers differ. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. An atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom. (3)
hints: For a neutral atom, electrons equal protons.
questions.solution:
Protons = 17 because atomic number is the proton number. [B1]
Electrons = 17 because the atom is neutral. [B1]
Neutrons = 35 - 17 = 18. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain the trend in reactivity down Group 1 of the periodic table. (4)
questions.solution:
Group 1 atoms react by losing one outer electron. [B1]
Down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. [B1]
The attraction between the nucleus and outer electron is weaker. [B1]
The electron is lost more easily, so reactivity increases. [B1]

topic: Bonding, structure, and the properties of matter

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid. (4)
hints: Compare ion mobility in solid and liquid states.
questions.solution:
Ionic compounds contain charged ions. [B1]
In a solid lattice the ions are fixed in position and cannot move. [B1]
When molten the ions are free to move. [B1]
Moving ions carry electric charge through the liquid. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. (4)
hints: How many bonds does each carbon make?
questions.solution:
Both are giant covalent forms of carbon. [B1]
In graphite each carbon forms three covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per carbon. [B1]
The delocalised electrons can move and carry charge. [B1]
In diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds so there are no free electrons or ions to carry charge. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain why metals are malleable and conduct electricity. (4)
hints: Different features explain malleability and conductivity.
questions.solution:
Metals consist of positive ions in a lattice surrounded by delocalised electrons. [B1]
Layers of metal ions can slide past one another while metallic bonding is maintained, so the metal is malleable. [B1]
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure. [B1]
The moving electrons carry electrical charge. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. A reaction in an open flask produces a gas. Explain why the measured mass of the flask and contents can decrease even though mass is conserved. (3)
hints: Mass is conserved for the whole system.
What can leave an open container?
questions.solution:
Atoms are not created or destroyed in the chemical reaction. [B1]
A gaseous product can leave the open flask. [B1]
The balance then measures only the material remaining in the flask, so the recorded mass decreases. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain why magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid but copper does not. (4)
hints: Use the position relative to hydrogen in the reactivity series.
questions.solution:
Magnesium is above hydrogen in the reactivity series. [B1]
Magnesium atoms lose electrons readily and can displace hydrogen from the acid. [B1]
Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. [B1]
Copper therefore does not displace hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Describe how to make pure, dry copper sulfate crystals from dilute sulfuric acid and insoluble copper oxide. (4)
hints: Use an excess of the insoluble base.
How do you remove the excess solid?
questions.solution:
Warm the dilute sulfuric acid. [B1]
Add copper oxide until some remains unreacted, showing the acid has been neutralised. [B1]
Filter to remove excess solid copper oxide. [B1]
Evaporate some water, allow the solution to cool and crystallise, then dry the crystals. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain the difference between an exothermic and an endothermic reaction using energy transfer to the surroundings. (4)
hints: State the direction of energy transfer.
questions.solution:
An exothermic reaction transfers energy from the reacting system to the surroundings. [B1]
The surroundings warm up and the measured temperature usually increases. [B1]
An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings. [B1]
The surroundings cool and the measured temperature usually decreases. [B1]

topic: The rate and extent of chemical change

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain why increasing temperature usually increases the rate of a chemical reaction. (4)
hints: Frequency alone is not the whole explanation.
questions.solution:
Particles move faster and have more kinetic energy. [B1]
Collisions occur more frequently. [B1]
A larger proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy. [B1]
Therefore there are more successful collisions per second. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Describe how the composition of Earth's atmosphere is thought to have changed since the early Earth. (4)
hints: Explain both the fall in carbon dioxide and rise in oxygen.

As Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form oceans. [B1]

Photosynthetic organisms released oxygen, causing oxygen concentration to rise. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how increasing concentrations of greenhouse gases can lead to climate change. (4)
hints: Explain the energy balance before the effects.
questions.solution:

They re-emit infrared radiation in all directions, including back towards the surface. [B1]
More energy is retained in the atmosphere, raising average global temperature. [B1]
Warming can change climate patterns, sea level and ecosystems. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how burning fuels can produce air pollutants and describe one effect of each of two pollutants. (4)
hints: Choose two pollutants and link source to effect.

questions.solution:

Sulfur impurities can form sulfur dioxide, which contributes to acid rain. [B1]
High-temperature engines can form nitrogen oxides, which contribute to acid rain and respiratory problems. [B1]
Particulates can damage lungs and contribute to global dimming. [B1]
